title: Hypernetworks for Dynamic Feature Selection
claim: Our method matches or beats leading baselines across feature-acquisition budgets, learning faster and reaching higher accuracy on diverse datasets.
layout: 3 panels in a row, left-to-right, shared legend style, dataset names below
description: Three side-by-side line plots, each for a different tabular dataset: (a) Diabetes, (b) Metabric, (c) Miniboone. The x-axis is the number of features acquired (0 to 10) and the y-axis is F1-macro. Each panel has the same five methods: VIP (yellow dashed), RePa (red dashed with diamonds), MoE (purple dash-dot), HyperDFS (light blue solid) and HyperEns (dark blue solid). All curves start from the same low value at zero features and rise as features are acquired. The blue proposed methods rise steeply and plateau near the top. In (a) HyperDFS clearly leads, while RePa lags badly. In (b) and (c) the curves converge to similar levels. A legend sits at the bottom right of each panel. The eye goes first to the blue curves.
caption: F1-macro according to the number of acquired features for the top-performing methods on three representative tabular datasets. Full acquisition curves for all datasets are provided in Appendix [ref].
abstract: Dynamic feature selection (DFS) is a machine learning framework in which features are acquired sequentially for individual samples under budget constraints. The exponential growth in the number of possible feature acquisition paths forces a DFS model to balance fitting specific scenarios against maintaining general performance, even when the feature space is moderate in size. In this paper, we study the structural limitations of existing DFS approaches to achieve an optimal solution. Then, we propose \textsc{Hyper-DFS}, a hypernetwork-based DFS approach that generates feature subset-specific classifier parameters on demand. We show that the use of hypernetworks compared to mask-embedding methods results in a smaller structural complexity bound. We also use a Set Transformer encoding to create a smooth conditioning space for the hypernetwork, so that functionally similar tasks are also geometrically close. In our benchmarks, \textsc{Hyper-DFS} performed best or second best compared to all state-of-the-art approaches on synthetic and real-life tabular data. It is also best or second best across all image datasets tested, and shows stronger zero-shot generalisation to feature subsets never seen during training than existing DFS approaches. Code available in: https://github.com/Fuminides/hyper_DFS
